Do jews have above average IQ? Short answer: I don't know.

Because, as I suspected, there has almost no (valid) research been done on the subject.

So let's dive in to the literature. A quick google scholar search on "iq jews" already shows a couple of things: not a lot of peer-reviewed research papers, and more importantly: not a lot of citations. This already indicates that not a lot of research has been done on this topic. But let´s continue, with the top hit: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0191886903000795

This is quite a good paper by Richard Lynn. In his introduction he goes in to previous studies, and criticizes them. In short his criticism of previous studies boils down to: 'small samples, and not representative of the population'. The intention of his study is to do the research, properly. He does an ok job regarding sample size, and acquiring a representative sample of the population. He does find a difference in IQ, but not as big as some have found before. Due to his accurate study design, one might say that his estimates are at least more valid than previous attempts. However, there is one big flaw in this study: the IQ estimates, and estimates in differences, are based on verbal IQ. The author does point out that verbal IQ correlates highly with IQ, even higher than other subtests related to IQ. However the author also mentioned in the introduction that previous studies have shown that jews have above average verbal IQ. Suppose jews and non-jews have the same average IQ, but differ on different IQ subtests, than only looking at the differences on a specific subtest will not say anything about the differences in IQ.

Note that this paper is the highest impact- and most cited (only 36 times though) peer-reviewed paper on this topic.

Now there have been some more studies on this topic. But they have the same problems, and also acknowledge these problems in previous studies: small sample sizes, and not representative of the population. When someone talks about high iq of jews, they are probably not talking about the ethiopian jews. That's a tricky thing about this research, because a specific jewish group is researched but the results are generalized to all "jews" (again, without a clear definition).
